newsitem.title: USA: Drug reduces ulcer bleeding and need for surgery.
newsitem.headline: Drug reduces ulcer bleeding and need for surgery.

text.p: A drug that shuts down the production of acid in the stomach can cut the risk of surgery or stomach bleeding for someone with an ulcer, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
But the research also suggests that the drug omeprazole is not effective when the ulcer has become so bad that fluid is oozing or blood is spurting from the wound.

In the United States, Europe and other developed regions of the world, doctors get to the stomach of a patient by putting a tube down the throat and treating the ulcer directly. The technique is known as endoscopy.

The new study, led by Dr. Mohammad Sultan Khuroo of the Sheri Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences in Kashmir, India, was an attempt to find an effective drug treatment for ulcers in developing areas of the world where endoscopy is not routinely available.

The Khuroo group took 220 volunteers whose ulcers had recently shown signs of bleeding and gave them either a placebo or the omeprazole, sold under the brand name Prilosec by the Astra Merck Group, joint venture between Swedish pharmaceutical giants Astra AB and its U.S. partner Merck and Cos., Inc.

"We found that omeprazole therapy was associated with significant reductions in the rates of further bleeding and surgical intervention, the number of days in the hospital, and the need for transfusion," the researchers concluded.

Only 11 percent of the omeprazole patients had further stomach bleeding, versus 36 percent who got the placebo. Twenty nine percent of the omeprazole recipients needed a transfusion compared to 71 percent in the placebo group.
However, among the patients whose ulcer was oozing or bleeding to begin with, the drug had no significant effect.

In an editorial, Drs. John R. Saltzman and John K. Zawacki of the University of Massachusetts Medical Center in Worcester, say the drug may be useful when endoscopy is not available, impractical, too risky, or the patient will not cooperate.
